source.title: Nonparametric regression using over-parameterized shallow ReLU neural networks

record.file_problem: Full text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper theoretically analyzes generalization of over-parameterized shallow ReLU networks on natural regression data, using risk bounds rather than the claim versions’ empirical comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical excess-risk bounds for constrained and regularized least-squares estimators. It does not report random-label fitting, standard gradient-method experiments, or comparisons among architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, or dropout. Its results do not test any listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper proves population excess-risk bounds for norm-constrained or regularized shallow ReLU regression estimators. None tests V1–V8. Width-independent upper bounds do not establish decreasing test error beyond interpolation (V2); Section 4 explicitly leaves the generalization of minimum-norm interpolators open.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: suitably constrained or regularized, sufficiently wide shallow ReLU least-squares estimators attain minimax-optimal convergence rates up to logarithmic factors for the specified regression classes. The paper does not establish these rates for unregularized interpolators or demonstrate that gradient training finds the required solutions.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical nonparametric regression analysis using constrained or penalized least squares; no empirical random-label experiment or standard gradient-method recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The bounds and required width depend on the regression function class and the stated weight constraint or regularization parameter.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 3 and 9 establish minimax-optimal population excess-risk rates up to logarithmic factors for sufficiently wide, constrained or regularized shallow ReLU regression estimators.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For bounded-response nonparametric regression over specified Hölder or variation classes, suitably norm-constrained or regularized shallow ReLU least-squares estimators achieve near-minimax excess-risk rates once sufficiently wide.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical rather than empirical and applies to specified regression classes and norm-constrained or regularized least squares. It does not establish behavior under standard gradient training or random-label memorization.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.

Whether widening beyond zero training error lowers test error under unregularized gradient training. The bounds require norm constraints or regularization and do not compare actual risks across widths.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification, local connectivity, and initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers and effects of tuning, weight decay, or switching optimizers.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover held-out performance.
Dropout effects, underfitting, training-set size, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Test-accuracy changes after removing highly memorized versus randomly selected examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical evidence can test a version, but these theorems address a different proposition. Section 4's discussion of interpolation and regularization supplies motivation and open questions, not a demonstrated qualification or refutation of V1 or V2.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label test accuracy.
A width sweep beyond interpolation and whether test error continues to fall.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning, weight decay, and language-model outcomes.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
